output.title: Trace one workflow before you automate anything
output.body:
Rethinking traceability is not about making every process visible. For a small business, it is usually about one recurring workflow where you keep asking: who did what, when, and why, and can I prove it quickly enough to act on it?

A practical place to look is the work that keeps coming back for manual checking: invoice-to-payment matching, a customer question to resolution log, or a refund dispute where the paper trail is spread across email, spreadsheets, and a payment tool. If you have to rebuild the story from scratch every time, the trace is already part of the cost.

The decision is bounded: compare the time spent tracing the record by hand with the risk of automating the wrong step. If the workflow is frequent, repetitive, and the audit trail matters later, traceability is worth examining. If the answer depends on judgment, exceptions, or payment approval, keep the human in the loop.

That boundary matters. Bareni requires human approval for money movement and other high-risk decisions. Automation can collect and organise the trail; it should not take the final call.

A useful next step is simple: pick one workflow and ask whether you could show the full chain of events today without rebuilding it from scratch. If not, start there.
